deployAtATime.note: The family 'deploy at <time>', matched in code and never sent to the model. AUTHORED, not generated: cardPhrasings.parsed carries one example and one near-miss, which is nowhere near enough to describe a family whose variable part is a TIME - one example would have the other platform build one spelling. The frame, after trimming, case-folding and removing a trailing . ! or ?: [please] deploy [it|this section] [today|tomorrow] at <time> [today|tomorrow] [please]. Anything else in the sentence - a section, a course, a weekday, a condition, a second request - falls through to the model. THE RULE THAT CARRIES THE MOST WEIGHT: a time with no am or pm must be written with two digits for the hour, because that is what 24-hour time looks like and it is the form schedule_deploy's own schema asks for. Measured on 2026-09-18: the smaller assistant sent 'Deploy at 6:30 AM' to deploy_section 10 trials out of 10, so a teacher who asked for half six tomorrow got a deploy to students on the spot (research/ai-assist/metal-routing-results.txt, issue #168). ASKED, NOT GUESSED (issue #194): a one-digit hour 1 to 9 with two digits of minutes and no am or pm - 'deploy at 6:30' - is morning or evening and nobody can tell which, so it is neither scheduled nor sent to the model: the app answers in code with wording.morningOrEvening, naming two sentences this family already accepts (the am one and the pm one, in the canonical form 'deploy [today |tomorrow ]at H:MM am|pm'), and the teacher types one of them. Nothing waits for the answer; the question and the teacher's sentence go into the conversation shown to the teacher and never into what the model is sent. wording.morningOrEvening is rendered for 'deploy at 6:30'; each asked row gives the clock and the two sentences for its own input, and each sentence must match this family to the when shown. Near-spellings are ASKED as well: a full stop for the colon ('deploy at 6.30'), a comma after the time ('deploy at 6:30, please'), and, since #277, a dotted two-digit hour 10 to 12 ('deploy at 10.30'), because each reached deploy_section 10 trials out of 10 when sent to the model (the #194 fix review, Qwen2.5-1.5B Q4_K_M, Apple M4 Pro). The clock is named back with a colon and the answers are built with one, so no such spelling is ever offered back. ANSWERED WITH THE SPELLING TO USE (issue #277): a time the family can read but does not set is answered in code with ONE sentence to type - wording.sayTheTimeAs, naming the time as written and the sentence, or wording.sayTheTimeAsWithoutTheComma when a comma is all that stands in the way - decided by running the matcher on the teacher's own sentence with its commas taken out and comparing the MOMENT it sets with the one the handed-back sentence sets, never by comparing text (sayItAs.expectOnlyDifference: spelling, theComma). A 'without please' form was ruled as well and is not built: taking 'please' out too was measured unreachable (0 of 113,400 sentences), because the frame already takes 'please' off either end. Nothing is set and nothing is sent to the model; the sentence handed back is built in the canonical form 'deploy [today |tomorrow ]at H:MM am|pm' and must match this family to expectWhen. Caught only for a REASON, of which there are three: a full stop between hour and minutes, one comma after the time (or before a part of the day), or a part of the day - 'in the morning', 'in the afternoon', 'in the evening', 'this morning', 'this afternoon', 'this evening', 'tonight', 'tomorrow morning', 'tomorrow afternoon', 'tomorrow evening' - after the time, or in front of 'at' ('deploy tonight at 6:30'; read by this step only, so what the frame ACCEPTS does not move). A day word the comma kept from the frame ('deploy at 6:30 pm tomorrow, please') is read as the frame's day word - and a one-digit time left on its own is then ASKED about ('deploy at 6:30 tomorrow, please'), as it is when the day word stands where the frame reads it. What is left must be a clock (hour, ':' or '.', two digits of minutes 0-59) with or without am/pm (joined or apart, dots allowed), or a bare hour beside am/pm or a part of the day. A part of the day is a WINDOW: morning 12 (12 am) and 1-11 (am), afternoon 12-5 (12 is noon, 1-5 pm), evening 5-11 (pm), tonight 5-11 (pm) and 12 as midnight (12 am, said with no day word, because midnight tonight is tomorrow). A two-digit hour with a leading zero, or 13-23, is 24-hour time and must fall inside the window (17:00 counts as both afternoon and evening). An hour outside its window is never respelled: a one-digit hour with no am or pm is ASKED about (the morningOrEvening question, keeping a day word only when the sentence said one plainly or the part of the day was 'tomorrow ...'); anything else is refused. With neither am/pm nor a part of the day, the hour must be two digits (the 24-hour reading); a one-digit hour there is already asked about, and a dotted 10 to 12 is asked. 'Today' and 'tonight' in one sentence agree, and tonight decides: the day word is dropped (so its midnight and its question carry none). A disagreement is refused, never resolved: am/pm against the part of the day, or a day word against the day the part of the day names. A spelling the family refuses for a reason of its own ('13:30 pm', '6:75 pm', 'deploy at 7') is not caught, and its refused row's reason stands. The frame is the same one accepted rows are read with, so anything the frame refuses is refused here too. accepted, asked, sayItAs and refused run the matcher (refused means neither answered, asked nor given a spelling: it goes to the model, and each refused row's why says what the model did with it where that was measured); resolving runs the settling step that turns a bare time into a whole moment, and is pure input to output with an injected clock so it means the same thing in any time zone.

echoedRequest.note: When the model's whole reply is the teacher's own sentence handed back, the app refuses the turn, says one honest sentence (wording.didNotFollowThat) and winds the turn back out of the conversation - the same rewind an unfinished answer gets. MEASURED, 2026-09-19, issue #215: Qwen2.5-1.5B Q4_K_M with the app's own server flags, request body and system prompt, temperature 0, the date line on every user message. "hide unit 4, day 20" came back word for word, date line and all, with no tool chosen. The echo was then KEPT in the history and the model copied the pattern it could see - user says X, assistant says X - so the very next request echoed too, including "Unpublish Unit 4, Day 20", a sentence the same model answers correctly every time in a FRESH conversation. Replayed on ICD2O and ICS4U, pages "Unit 4, Day 20" and "Unit 4, Day 21": identical in all four. One unrecognised phrase made the window useless until it was closed and opened again, so the rewind is the half that cures it rather than reports it. THE RULE: no tool call in the reply, and the reply's text equals the turn's own user message - compared case-folded and with . ! ? trimmed from both ends. Both spellings of the question count: the message AS SENT (with the date line) and the sentence the teacher typed, because a model that trims the parenthetical is not a different fault. The message compared is the one at the START of the turn, never the last user message anywhere - that is what makes a card-matched second lap safe by construction, since such a turn begins with a TOOL RESULT and so has no user message in it at all. STRICT ON PURPOSE, and here is what that misses: an echo with a preamble ("Sure: hide unit 4, day 21"), a partial echo, and any other kind of residue in the history. Each would need a similarity measure, and a fuzzy rule that fires on a legitimate answer is worse than the fault - it would throw a real reply away and tell the teacher it did not follow. The one corner it leaves is a teacher typing a content-free token ("ok") to which the model replies with the same token; they read one honest sentence instead, and nothing can be lost, because everything carrying state is a button or a sheet rather than free text. NOT EXPRESSIBLE AS A SCENARIO: the scenario runner builds its agent with no engine behind it, so a model reply cannot be scripted - the same limit windowBinding records. These cases are the predicate; a platform runs them against its own reader of (what was sent, what came back, whether there was a tool call).

hideIsUnpublish.note: "Hide" means what "unpublish" means, and it is answered in CODE rather than by the model. Measured on 2026-09-19 (issue #215): Qwen2.5-1.5B Q4_K_M, the app's own server flags, request body and system prompt, temperature 0, an ICS4U section window. "unpublish unit 4, day 21" reached unpublish_pages every time; "hide unit 4, day 21" reached NO tool at all, in five phrasings out of five - the model handed the teacher their own sentence back as text, date line and all. It errs in the safe direction and it reads as broken. Steering the model with a sentence in a tool description was REJECTED: one clarifying sentence added to publish_pages' description once took the promise-card score from 110/110 to 90/110 and broke three probes that had been perfect, because a small model reads a description naming another tool as a recommendation rather than a boundary. So the frame lives in code and the router never sees these sentences. THE VERB GATES THE WHOLE FRAME, not only the day arm: hide and unpublish take a whole unit or one class page AND tolerate the spellings listed at the end of this note, while publish is read by a separate frame that has not moved - the literal opening "publish unit " and a bare number. So "publish unit 4, day 3" still goes to the model, and so do "publish unit 4?", "please publish unit 4", "publish unit 4 please", "publish  unit 5" and "publish unit, 4", every one of them a refused row below. The split was made deliberately rather than inherited: the first version of this frame read the verb AFTER stripping the courtesy words and the question mark, and an adversarial differential fuzz of 13,464 sentences across the old matcher and the new one found 0 matches lost and 141 NEW publish_pages matches, none of them asked for. "publish unit 4?" is the case that decided it - a teacher typing a question mark is plausibly ASKING, and that sentence would have published a whole unit with no model in the loop, which is the same ambiguity this note uses below to reject "show unit 4". Unpublishing errs safe - a page nobody can see - while publishing puts a page in front of students, and "Publish Unit 2, Day 3" is answered correctly by the small model 10 trials out of 10, so there is nothing to buy by widening the dangerous direction on the same day. "show" and "unhide" are out for a nearer reason: "show unit 4" is at least as likely to mean "display it to me", and getting that wrong publishes. THE REFUSALS ARE THE SAFETY HALF. A matched card binds THIS window's course and section into the call unconditionally, and the guard that refuses a request naming another course runs only on the model's answers - so a frame that swallowed "hide unit 4, day 21 in ICS3U" would act on this window's course and report success, which is the failure a teacher cannot catch. The frame therefore reads a fixed number of words and refuses anything else, including a negation and a sentence naming two pages. TERM-BLIND, deliberately and for now: only the literal word "unit" is matched, because the matcher is a pure function of the sentence and a course's own word for a unit is not in it. A Module course loses nothing - "hide module 4, day 21" falls through to the model exactly as it does today, and "hide unit 4" still works there because the planner accepts "unit" alongside the course's own word. Spellings are the whole question for a frame like this, so they are written out here rather than left to one example: commas are read as frame punctuation and dropped before the words are counted (the same reading make_room_for_classes uses), a trailing question mark comes off, and "please" is courtesy at either end.

A teacher who rolls over, ignores the question and comes back to ask again arrives with the dates already right — so the plan twin has nothing to propose, and returning "already on the day it should be" ended the turn there: asking before changing is ON by default and the surface returns early on anything that is not a plan, so the real call never ran and the teacher read nothing whatever about the website while the section stayed pinned to last year's site. With that setting turned OFF the same request was asked properly, which is what makes it a defect rather than a limitation: the question existed or not depending on a setting. The teacher line in the middle is load-bearing — it anchors the two sentences after it to the SECOND turn, and without it the first turn's reply satisfies them and the case cannot fail. `when` is "say" because the last turn is ANSWERED, not proposed: nothing is waiting to be agreed to, and a card there would offer a Go that changes nothing.

cases.name: deploy with a preview running
cases.why: The window's Deploy button stops any running preview first and waits for it to finish: stop mode finds a section's processes by working directory and would take the deploy's build with it.

cases.name: deploy with no preview running
cases.why: Nothing to stop. The reply says nothing about a preview either way — an assistant that accounts for what it had to do in order to obey is talking about itself.

cases.name: deploy with no section window open
cases.why: There is no button to press. This is the path Claude Code over MCP takes, and a deploy scheduled for half six in the morning. It must ask the same place for its launcher arguments as the button does, or a Cloudflare course goes to Netlify.

cases.name: deploy while that section is already busy
cases.why: A refusal in a whole sentence. The menu fragment that sits under a greyed-out menu item says nothing when read out in a conversation. Note the event: the assistant DOES press Deploy — the window is what declines, which is the real shape of it. This case was written expecting no event at all, and running it said otherwise.

cases.name: the deploy card is agreed to
cases.why: What the teacher chose is part of the history, in their own bubble. A conversation where the assistant asked, nothing answered, and something plainly happened is worse than one you cannot read back at all.

cases.name: the deploy card is cancelled
cases.why: The fact, and nothing else. Read which kind of card is pending BEFORE clearing it.

cases.name: an immediate deploy's card still asks the immediate question
cases.why: The other half of the split made for issue #184 (2026-09-23): a SCHEDULED deploy's card asks wording.scheduleQuestion, and this pins that an IMMEDIATE deploy's card still asks wording.deployQuestion - so the question is chosen by which deploy it is, on both platforms, rather than one question replacing the other. The choice is keyed on the tool's NAME: a third tool that waits for approval would get wording.deployQuestion, the reading that is safe for anything that deploys. Declined rather than approved so that nothing is deployed.

cases.name: a plan card is cancelled
cases.why: Here the reassurance IS the answer: the plan described changes to pages, so whether they happened is the part in doubt.

cases.name: a page edit, with a preview running
cases.why: The stop sits beside the WRITES, not beside the start: a preview left serving while the pages beneath it are rewritten serves a half-changed site, and the teacher's next refresh is a race they cannot see they are in. No expectReply on purpose — the reply is about the pages that changed, not about the preview; this case was written claiming the preview sentence, and running it said otherwise.

cases.name: a deploy asked for at a time is answered in code and asks about the MOMENT
cases.why: Measured on 2026-09-18: the smaller assistant sent this sentence to deploy_section 10 trials out of 10, so a teacher who asked for half six tomorrow got a deploy to students on the spot, behind an approval card that mentioned no time at all. Answered in code it cannot reach the model, and the card it does reach names the section, the destination and the whole moment. 'Section 1' is what is asserted because it is LOCALE-FREE and appears in the scheduled card on both platforms while appearing in the immediate one on neither: a formatted time is written '6:30 AM' here, '6:30 a.m.' on another Mac and with a different separator again in a 24-hour locale, so asserting one would pin the machine rather than the behaviour. The MOMENT is pinned instead by deployAtATime.resolving, which is pure and portable. Declined rather than approved because approving would write a real scheduled job. The question under the card is wording.scheduleQuestion, not wording.deployQuestion (issue #184, 2026-09-23): the immediate question reads as 'now' under a card that has just named a later moment. The sentence wording.scheduleQuestion carries is a first draft, marked for Russell's wording pass; this case names it by key, so the pass can change it freely.

cases.name: a time that could be morning or evening is asked about in code, and nothing is scheduled
cases.why: Issue #194. 'deploy at 6:30' is morning or evening and nobody can tell which, so it is refused by the deploy-at-a-time family - and until this it went to the model instead, which answered that shape of sentence with a deploy to students on the spot (the smaller assistant, 10 trials out of 10 for 'Deploy at 6:30 AM', 2026-09-18). Now it is asked about IN CODE: the reply is wording.morningOrEvening, nothing is scheduled, and 'say' makes a card on this turn the failure. A runner with no model reachable still passes, because the model is never asked; on the old behaviour the line is never written. What the model is sent is not in the transcript, so each platform also pins in its own suite that the teacher's sentence and the question never reach it.

cases.name: answering the morning-or-evening question with the sentence it named puts the scheduled card up
cases.why: The other half of the question: the answer is a sentence it NAMED, and that sentence is answered in code on the very next turn, with the scheduled card and its question. A question whose suggested answer the app did not understand would be worse than no question. Declined rather than approved because approving would write a real scheduled job; the whole moment is pinned by deployAtATime.resolving.

cases.name: a time the app can read but does not set is answered with the spelling to use, and nothing is scheduled
cases.why: Issue #277. 'deploy at 6.30 pm' names a time the family can read but does not set (a full stop is not its clock separator), and until this it went to the model, which answered it with a deploy to students on the spot 10 trials out of 10 (the #194 fix review, Qwen2.5-1.5B Q4_K_M, Apple M4 Pro). Now it is answered IN CODE with the one sentence to type: the reply is wording.sayTheTimeAs, nothing is scheduled, and 'say' makes a card on this turn the failure. A runner with no model reachable still passes, because the model is never asked; on the old behaviour the line is never written. What the model is sent is not in the transcript, so each platform also pins in its own suite that the teacher's sentence and the reply never reach it.

cases.name: answering with the sentence the spelling reply named puts the scheduled card up
cases.why: The other half: the sentence the reply NAMED is answered in code on the very next turn, with the scheduled card and its question. A reply whose sentence the app did not understand would send the teacher's next turn to the model - the thing it exists to prevent. Declined rather than approved because approving would write a real scheduled job; the whole moment is pinned by deployAtATime.resolving.

cases.name: "hide" is answered in code and puts the unpublish plan up
cases.why: Measured on 2026-09-19 (issue #215): the smaller assistant answered "hide unit 4, day 21" with no tool at all - five phrasings out of five, the teacher's own sentence handed back as text - while answering the same request worded "unpublish" correctly every time. So the word is answered in code, and this case is what proves the whole path a card phrasing unlocks rather than just the match: the scenario runner builds the agent with NO engine behind it, so a sentence that reached the model here could not be answered at all. Approved rather than said, because confirmation before acting is on in the fixture and unpublish_pages has a plan twin, so the turn ends on a card - "say" would fail by construction. The three lines are the portable ones: the teacher's sentence, the question the card asks, and their Go. The outcome sentence is deliberately NOT pinned - it is built in the runner rather than being an AssistWording key on either platform, so asserting it would hold one app to the other's phrasing. ONE THING THIS CASE NEEDS THAT THE OTHERS DO NOT: a PUBLISHED "Unit 1, Day 1" in the fixture. `pending: unpublish_pages` has nothing to propose otherwise, so no card appears and the failure reads as the phrasing not matching when it is the fixture that is empty. Said here rather than in one platform's harness because a runner that sets up only publish_class_on and re_date_classes will meet this the day it implements the frame, and lose an afternoon to it.

scenarios.note: What must happen, and in what ORDER. The order is the assertion: every wrong ordering still passes a test that only checks all three events occurred. Event names are this contract's own; map them to whatever your app calls them. `given.saying` is a CONVERSATION — what the teacher types, in order, each turn settled before the next — because some behaviour exists only across turns; when it is absent a single turn is run, using whichever fixed phrasing reaches `given.pending`. `when` says what the teacher does on the LAST turn: "approve" presses Go on the card that is waiting (and fails if none is), "decline" presses Cancel, "say" means the last turn is ANSWERED rather than proposed, so nothing is waiting and a card there is the failure the case exists to catch; anything else is a tool name, called directly. `expectTranscriptContains` matches each named line by speaker PREFIX and sentence SUBSTRING, in order but not necessarily adjacent, and a line may satisfy more than one expectation — one reply often composes several named sentences into a single bubble. A literal line that is not a `wording.` name is matched as written, which is how a case anchors later expectations to a particular TURN.

tools.note: Three lists, deliberately. `all` is what the runner can execute; `local` is what the small model is SHOWN (the plan twins and remember_timetable are taken off, because the model never has to name a plan and dates it supplies are dates it may have invented); `mcpOnly` is the ten offered to Claude Code on top of everything — three asking for judgement about meaning, the rest either never needed by a model scoped to one section or already reachable by it through a fixed phrasing.
tools.planTwinsNote: A write with a twin is shown as a plan first. Four writes have none, deliberately: rebuild_preview changes no page, undo_last_change IS the remedy, deploy_section waits on its own button whatever plan mode says, and a cancelled scheduled deploy is remedied by scheduling it again.

absentHere.rejected: Adding it for symmetry. There is no boolean anywhere on this surface at all; the last was includeLinked, which asked the MODEL how far a publish or an unpublish should reach — the exact reasoning this design exists to keep out of a router. The rules live in AssistPublishPlanner instead, where they are written down once and tested.
absentHere.why: On Windows a batch of edits can be made with the preview suppressed and rebuilt once at the end. Here every change rebuilds, which is what the assistant's own system prompt promises a teacher, so there is nothing for the flag to mean.

departures.advertisedNotAccepted: The separator is what the SCHEMA tells the model, not the only character the runner accepts. AssistToolRunner is deliberately forgiving and splits on several — pages on semicolon or newline, codes and dates on comma, semicolon, newline and more. So a difference recorded here is a difference in what each side TELLS the model, which is worth knowing; it is not necessarily an incompatibility, and a suite should not assert one from it.
departures.howToReadThis: Each entry says a parameter is a string carrying a list, on which surfaces, and the separator this surface ADVERTISES to the model. It does NOT say what the other platform does — the mac cannot check that. A suite seeing both should intersect this list with its own schemas, and there are FOUR outcomes, not three: an ARRAY there is a real type departure; a string there with a DIFFERENT separator is a separator difference, worth asserting deliberately; a string there with the SAME separator is an agreement and nothing should be asserted about it; anything else is a real disagreement. Leaving the third case out turns a suite red for an agreement, which is how this note first read.
departures.note: How this surface's schemas differ from the Windows server's. Emitted so that side can READ them instead of keeping a hand-written copy — the copy is what made the two surfaces drift in the first place.
departures.notEnumeratedHere: Arguments the Windows server takes that this surface does not DECLARE. Mostly extra parameters on tools BOTH platforms serve — re_date_classes and read_remembered_timetable are the clearest, with the same name and different parameters on the two servers (GUI-IMPROVEMENTS.md row 447). Said precisely because the first version of this key said they were tools the mac does not serve at all, which is false: it serves both. The reason they stay in that platform's own list is that the mac does not declare those arguments, so it can neither test them nor notice when they change.

cases.why: The reason the binding exists at all: "Unpublish Unit 4, Day 12" is read as section 4, and the teacher is told their course has no Section 4. A perfectly reasonable misreading of a page name that begins with a number, reported twice before it was fixed.

An ABSENT section is bound too. No tool reads an omission as "every section", so a call that left it out is simply a lost turn - refused by the tool with a complaint that reads as though the teacher's own sentence were the problem.

The same course in another casing is not another course, so the turn runs - and the WINDOW's spelling is what runs. The approval card a teacher reads before pressing Go prints the code verbatim, so leaving the model's casing would put "deploy ics3u Section 1" in front of them.

A different course, and it is in this working folder. Nothing runs: no plan, no approval card, no tool. Binding it to this window instead would publish an ICS3U class and report success, which is the one failure a teacher cannot catch. The sentence names both courses and says to open that one.
The refusal holds for READS as well. Allowing them was REJECTED: a teacher cannot tell which tool the model picked, so a rule that held only for writes would read as random.

A typo, or a code the model invented: it names no course here. REFUSED rather than bound to this window, which is the decision worth writing down, because binding it looks harmless - a code matching nothing cannot reach another course - and would publish an ICS3U class off "publish MCV4's class". A second sentence rather than the first, because the first ends by telling the teacher to open that course and there is no such course to open.

Its schema declares NEITHER argument, so neither is the window's to take back and there is nothing to refuse - the tool ignores both. The case is here to pin the gate on the schema rather than on a list of tools. NOTE for a second implementation: `runs` cannot be observed from outside on the mac, because the tool reads neither argument and there is no plan card to hold them; the mac asserts that the tool RAN and that the turn was not refused. Assert whatever your own seam can see.

Refused like any other differing code - and the sentence names that course the way the WORKING FOLDER spells it, not the way the model wrote it. A teacher told to open "mcv4u" is being sent to look for something their sidebar does not show. The same courtesy the window's OWN code already gets when it reaches the approval card. Only for a course that is here: when the folder has no such course there is nothing else to show, so askedAboutACourseThatIsNotHere carries the model's own text, trimmed.

windowBinding.note: An assistant window is opened for ONE section of ONE course. Given that window and the arguments the MODEL wrote on its tool call, these say what actually runs - or which refusal the teacher reads instead, and - where a case says so - which SPELLING of the other course that refusal puts in front of the teacher. AUTHORED, and preserved across `Plantoir --write-contracts`. The rule in one sentence: the SECTION is always the window's, present or absent, and the COURSE is the window's or the turn was refused. Gated on the TOOL'S OWN SCHEMA declaring the argument, never on a list of tool names - today the schema and a list of twelve would agree, which is exactly when a list looks harmless. Only the MODEL's calls are bound this way; a client driving the tools directly over MCP chooses its own course and section, and nothing here applies to it.
